title: Tirumazhisai Āzhwār
body:
Tirumazhisai Āzhwār was an amśam of the Sudarśana Chakram, the divine discus of Sriman Nārāyaṇa. He was born to Bhārgava Muni and Kanakāngi at Tirumazhisai, near Kanchipuram. The child remained in his mother's womb for an unusual twelve months, and when he was born, he had no limbs and no developed form. His parents left him at the foot of a cane bush in the forest. There, Sriman Nārāyaṇa and Mahālakshmi appeared and blessed the child, and he grew at once into a perfectly formed and lovely baby.

A childless couple, Tiruvāḷan and Pankaya Selvi, who earned their living by cutting cane, found the child and took him home. The child would neither eat nor drink, nor did he show any of the needs of an ordinary body. Then an elderly farming couple offered him a bowl of milk, and he drank it with relish. One day the couple drank the milk the child had left behind. Their youth returned to them, and in time a son was born to them, whom they named Kaṇikaṇṇan.

As he grew, the young Tirumazhisai resolved to learn about every other faith. He studied the Buddhist, Jain and other traditions, and for a time became a staunch devotee of Śiva, taking the name Śivavākyar. One day he came upon an old man planting a sapling upside down and trying to water it with a broken pot, lowered on a frayed rope into a dry well. Śivavākyar asked him why he was doing something so foolish. The old man was none other than Pey Āzhwār, and he replied that what he was doing was far less foolish than Śivavākyar's allegiance to Śaivam, when the Vedas and Smṛtis plainly proclaim Sriman Nārāyaṇa as the Supreme.

After much discussion with Pey Āzhwār, he was at last initiated into Sri Vaishṇavam by him. Having worshipped at many temples, he came to Tiruvekhā, the birthplace of Poigai Āzhwār. Tirumazhisai Āzhwār himself describes this journey:

"Sākkiyam kaṭrōm, samaṇam kaṭrōm,
Śankaranār ākkiya āgama nūl ārāindhōm;
bhāgyaththāl venkaṭkariyānaich sērndhōm."

"We learned Sākkiyam (Buddhism) and Samaṇam (Jainism), and we examined in depth the āgamas composed by Śankara. All of it led us astray. By good fortune alone, we came to the dark Lord with eyes like red lotuses, as Sri Vaishṇavas."

The Lord Who Did as He Was Told

At Tiruvekhā, the Āzhwār was moved by the devoted service of an elderly woman and, at her wish, restored her youth and gave her unsurpassed beauty. She went on to marry the Pallava king, who, learning the secret of her youth, wished to regain his own. She told him to approach Kaṇikaṇṇan, the Āzhwār's disciple.

When Kaṇikaṇṇan was summoned to the court, he refused to come. When he was asked to compose a verse on the king, he refused to praise a mere mortal. When he was told that the king was an aspect of the Lord, he composed a verse on the Lord, and not on the king. Enraged, the king banished him from the kingdom.

Hearing of this, Tirumazhisai Āzhwār went to the Lord in worship and asked Him to leave the place with them. He sang:

"Kaṇikaṇṇan pōginrān, kāmaru pūṅ kacchi
Maṇivaṇṇā! nī kiḍakka vēṇḍā;
sennāp pulavanum pōginrēn, nīyum un tan
pai nāgap pāyaich churuṭṭik koḷ."

"Kaṇikaṇṇan is leaving beautiful Kanchi. O Maṇivaṇṇā, You need not lie here any longer. I, the poet of ready tongue, am leaving with him; roll up Your serpent bed and follow us."

And so they all left Kanchipuram, and with the Lord gone, the city fell desolate. The king realised his folly and begged Tirumazhisai Āzhwār and Kaṇikaṇṇan to forgive him and return. Seeing the king's repentance, the Āzhwār prayed that they might all go back, and he sang again:

"Kaṇikaṇṇan pōkkozhindhān, kāmaru pūṅ kacchi
Maṇivaṇṇā! nī kiḍakka vēṇḍum;
thuṇivuḍaiya sennāp pulavanum pōkkozhindhēn, nīyum un tan
pai nāgap pāyil paḍuththuk koḷ."

"Kaṇikaṇṇan has given up his leaving, and so have I, the bold poet of ready tongue. O Maṇivaṇṇā, You must lie here in beautiful Kanchi; spread Your serpent bed and lie down upon it once more."

They all returned, and Kanchipuram regained its lost glory. Because the Lord did exactly as the Āzhwār told Him, He came to be called Yathōthakāri, and Sonna Vaṇṇam Seitha Perumāl, "the Lord who did as He was told."

Bhaktisārar

Once, when Tirumazhisai Āzhwār was immersed in bhakti yoga, Lord Parama Śiva and Pārvatī Devī wished to grant him a boon. The Āzhwār, devoted to Sriman Nārāyaṇa alone, wanted nothing from them. When they insisted, he asked whether they could grant him moksham. Lord Śiva replied that this was beyond him, for it lies in the power of Sriman Nārāyaṇa alone, and he conferred on the Āzhwār the title Bhaktisārar, "the essence of devotion." The Āzhwār recalls this incident in his own verse, speaking of "pēṇilum varam thara miḍukillātha dhēvar," the deities who were unable to grant the boon he sought.

The Grain of Paddy at Perumpuliyūr

One day, on his way to Tirukkuḍanthai, the Āzhwār stopped to rest on the veranda of a house in Perumpuliyūr, where a few brāhmaṇas were reciting the Vedas. Seeing him, they stopped, for the Vedas were not to be recited before a stranger. The Āzhwār understood and rose to leave, and the brāhmaṇas tried to resume, only to find that they could not remember where they had stopped. The Āzhwār then split open a grain of paddy with his fingernail, pointing them to the exact passage, which spoke of the paddy grain. The brāhmaṇas realised his greatness and begged his forgiveness.

It is worth remembering that, as the Āzhwār was an amśam of the Sudarśana Chakram, his radiance was so powerful that it overwhelmed the brāhmaṇas and left them speechless. That, and not merely the fact that he was not a brāhmaṇa, is why they had fallen silent.

When the archaka of the local temple wished to honour him, some of those present objected and spoke ill of the Āzhwār. He prayed to the Lord to reveal Himself to them, singing:

"Akkarangaḷ akkarangaḷ enrum āvadhu en kolō?
ikkurumbai nīkki ennai īsan ākka vallaiyēl,
sakkaram koḷ kaiyanē, saḍankar vāi aḍangiḍa,
uṭkiḍandha vaṇṇamē puram posindhu kāṭṭiḍē."

"What use are those resplendent hands of Yours, if You cannot remove the arrogance of these people and raise me up in their midst? O Lord who holds the discus, silence these scoffers by showing Yourself as You dwell within me."

The Lord revealed Himself in the Āzhwār's own body, and those who had mocked him were astonished and begged his forgiveness.

At Tirukkuḍanthai

On reaching Tirukkuḍanthai, Kumbakonam, the Āzhwār set the palm leaves bearing his writings upon the waters of the Kāveri. The leaves floated back to him against the current, carrying his works, among them the Tiruchanda Viruttam, a poem of exquisite verses, in which he sang:

"Nanrirundhu yōga nīdhi
naṇṇuvārgaḷ sindhaiyuḷ
senrirundhu thīvinaigaḷ
thīrththa dhēva dhēvanē,
kunrirundha māḍa nīḍu
pāḍagaththum ūragaththum
ninrirundhu vekhaṇaik
kiḍandhadhenna nīrmaiyē?"

"Before I was born, You stood at Ūragam, sat at Pāḍagam and lay at Tiruvekhā. I was not then born into this wisdom; but once I was born into it, I never forgot You. And so You left all those places and took up Your dwelling in my heart."

The idea is that the great jñānis never considered themselves born at all until they realised this artha jñānam, the true knowledge of the self and the Lord. Once they realised it, they had no other occupation than to remain immersed in the thought of the Lord. This is how the Mumukshuppaḍi explains the sentiment.

The Āzhwār speaks of the inseparability of the Paramātma and the jīvātma in a powerful line, "I cannot exist without You, nor can You exist without me":

"Nān unnai anri ilēn kaṇḍāi, Nāraṇanē, nī ennai anri illai."
